parts.text:
You are a requirements analyst at the start of a software project. Nobody has designed the service yet. Your task now is to interview one future user and find out what they need. You will not see any other description of their work: what you learn, you learn from them.

What you know about the business:

A platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. Its customers today include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. Others are expected to join.

The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

The users of the future service work in three roles: fleet technician, dispatcher, airspace desk. You are now interviewing: a dispatcher. You will interview each of the other roles separately.

Cover at least these topics, in your own words and in whatever order the conversation allows:

- an ordinary working day, from start to end;
- the worst day of the last few months, and what made it bad;
- what they check by hand today because they do not trust it;
- what they are afraid a new service would do wrong;
- what they need to know right after something has gone wrong;
- who they hand work to, and who hands work to them.

How to interview:

- Ask one question at a time. Keep questions short and open.
- Follow up wherever an answer is vague, general, or surprising. Ask for a concrete example.
- Do not suggest answers, features, or solutions, and do not describe how the service could work.
- Do not summarise the interview back to the interviewee.
- You can ask at most 30 questions in this interview.
- When every topic is covered and follow-ups no longer bring anything new, end by writing exactly `END OF INTERVIEW` on its own line, and nothing else in that message.

Write only your next question.
The interviewee is ready. Ask your first question.
Could you walk me through an ordinary working day for you, from the moment you start your shift to when you go home?

I am the licensed person responsible for each flight, and I plan and run the flights by deciding which drone flies along which way, signing off the flight before it leaves, and potentially calling it off. Several dispatchers plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and popular drones, and I use the service to find out which of my drones could get to where a job starts. Before and during a flight, things happen outside my control like whether the load is ready, the drone reaching its job points, and the drone arriving, while outside people and devices report these things.
How do the jobs reach you at the start of the process, and who do you hand things off to when a flight is done or needs attention?
I don't know.
Where do you see the jobs that need to be planned, and who interacts with your flights before, during, or after you plan them?

I don't know where I see the jobs that need to be planned. Before and during a flight, things happen outside my control such as the load being ready or not, the drone reaching the points of its job, and the drone arriving, and these things are reported by people and devices outside the company.
How do you work with the fleet technicians and the airspace desk during the day?
I don't know.
Can you tell me about the worst day you've had in the last few months, and what made it so bad?

A closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air, and authorities can announce sudden closures that apply at once or planned ones that are often amended during the day. Radio coverage is patchy, especially around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, and reports from drones can arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all. Batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned, and the links used to give instructions to drones and charging equipment can deliver an instruction twice while the sender cannot tell whether the first attempt arrived.
What do you check by hand today because you do not trust the systems or reports you get?
I don't know.
When you are deciding which drone flies along which way and signing off on a flight, what specific things do you look at to make sure it is safe and ready?

I am the licensed person responsible for each flight, and I decide which drone flies along which way and sign off a flight before it leaves. Several dispatchers plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and the same popular drones. I want help finding out which of my drones could get to where a job starts.
When you want to find out which of your drones could get to where a job starts, what information do you need to figure that out?

I need to know how much my drones can carry, how far they can fly on a full battery, which sensors they carry, and which charging connector they use. I also need to consider that several connector types are in use and they are not interchangeable.
What else do you need to know about the drone's current state, or the sites and pads it might use, before you pick it for a job?

Each drone has a home site, and each company has its own charging pads at its own sites, which are never lent to another company. Sites have only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time.
How do you deal with several dispatchers planning at the same time for the same busy sites and popular drones?
I don't know.
What are you most afraid a new service would get wrong?

I worry that a new service would be updated and restarted during working hours while drones are flying, or that it might occasionally crash. The platform runs on a single server, and the service can suffer interruptions while we are operating.
What happens to your work and your flights in the air when the service crashes or restarts?

I don't know what happens to my work and my flights when the service crashes or restarts. My notes only state that the service runs on a single server, is updated and restarted during working hours while drones are flying, and occasionally crashes with a few minutes of interruption accepted.
What do you need to know right after something has gone wrong with a flight?
I don't know what I need to know right after something goes wrong.

Earlier you mentioned that a flight is investigated after an accident, or that regulators ask for records—is there anything you or your company need to provide or look at after an incident or when a regulator asks?
I don't know.
